content: Hi all. Lean noob here. How can I find out what the 'state of the art' is when it comes to Lean 4 and infinite Ramsey theory, as well as set theory more generally? I know of LeanExplore, LeanSearch, and the Mathlib docs.
Ah ok thank you, so this is just the basic Ramsey's Theorem.

Is there a clever way of searching for relevant papers? For example I see that independence of CH has been formalised before (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02901), but I can't seem to find it on Mathlib.
Some semantic search tools might be helpful as well. Here is a blog post details several other ways of searching for Lean material, in case you would find it useful.

One thing that may help is that searching mathlib only gives part of the picture: quite a lot of research-level Lean work lives in standalone projects.

In particular, the CH independence formalisation you linked is the Flypitch project, which was a standalone Lean 3 development rather than something merged into current mathlib. The main theorem there is independence_of_CH in src/summary.lean, so that explains why searching present-day mathlib doesn't turn it up.

For trying to work out the "state of the art", I'd probably search at several levels:

  • mathlib / LeanSearch / docs for material already in the main library;

  • the Lean community's Lean projects page, which indexes standalone projects and also has a project-intentions registry;

  • Reservoir for other Lean packages;

  • the community's Lean papers bibliography for formalisation papers;

  • GitHub/Zulip searches for projects that may not have made it into any index yet.

For set theory specifically, another substantial current Lean 4 project worth looking at is ConNF, formalising the consistency of New Foundations. Mathlib also has the Mathlib/SetTheory/ZFC/ hierarchy.

So I wouldn't interpret “not on LeanSearch” as “not formalised”; for research-level material it can instead mean “lives in a separate repository”, or sometimes “was done in Lean 3 and was never ported”.
Note that Flypitch was recently ported to Lean 4 as part of the recent autoformalization of Erdos 501, which could be found by searching on Palomar
